title: Which Way Does It Run?
objective: After this level you can spot reverse causation, where the supposed effect is really the cause.
summary: Sometimes the supposed effect is the cause. Reversing causation is a false cause fallacy; checking which came first can rule a cause out.

cards.headline: Whenever the streets fill with umbrellas, it rains. Do umbrellas bring rain?
cards.body: Obviously not: the rain brings out the umbrellas. Put like that, it's a joke. But the same backwards step hides inside plenty of serious-sounding claims, and it's much harder to spot when you don't already know which way the arrow points.

cards.headline: Reversing causation
cards.body: Reversing causation means drawing a causal conclusion with cause and effect swapped. It's another false cause fallacy. A logic encyclopedia gives this example: every officer at one company owns a big boat, so if you want to become an officer, get a bigger boat. The arrow runs the other way. Being an officer brings the high income that buys the boat.

cards.headline: The chocolate, reversed
cards.body: Messerli raised this reading of his own chocolate data. Perhaps sharper minds lead to more chocolate, not the other way round: people with superior cognitive function might know more about dark chocolate's health benefits and eat more of it. He even noted that winning a Nobel Prize might trigger a burst of chocolate eating, though most likely a brief one.

cards.headline: Check the order
cards.body: One clue helps a lot: a cause must come before its effect, since effects never come before their causes. So ask what came first. The boat, or the promotion? Timing alone can't prove a cause, as Level 43's rooster showed. But when the supposed cause turns out to come second, the timing rules it out.

mascot.line: People mix these up: coming first can't prove a cause, but coming second rules one out.

cards.headline: Direction: checked
learned: Reversing causation swaps cause and effect
A cause that comes second is ruled out

questions.prompt: What does the reversing causation mistake get wrong?

options.label: It counts a coincidence as a cause
It swaps the cause and the effect
It ignores a third factor behind both
It blames one cause among many

questions.explanation: Reversing causation treats the effect as the cause: the boat as the route to the job, instead of the job paying for the boat.

questions.prompt: With the arrows running the right way, match each effect with its cause.
questions.explanation: The rain brings out the umbrellas. Being an officer brings the income that buys the boat. And winning a Nobel Prize might trigger a burst of chocolate eating.

questions.prompt: Which reverse-causation reading did Messerli offer for his chocolate data?

options.label: Sharper minds might lead to eating more chocolate
Chocolate might make people much better scientists
options.rationale: That's the direct reading, chocolate causing prizes.

options.label: Cold climates might drive both chocolate and prizes
options.rationale: That's a confounder reading, a third factor.

options.label: The link might be a coincidence of small numbers
options.rationale: Coincidence is a different explanation, not a reversal.

questions.explanation: Y influencing X: people with superior cognitive function might eat more chocolate, not the other way round.
